strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: absolute, gravity-referenced camera control for text-to-video generation, as opposed to relative/first-frame-anchored conditioning used in prior work (AC3D, CameraCtrl, etc.).

Creative and technically sound data pipeline that leverages 360° panoramic videos to synthesize diverse camera trajectories (including rare shots like Dutch angles and extreme pitches) that are largely absent from standard video datasets such as RealEstate10K, with clear empirical evidence of the resulting distributional diversity (Fig. 5).

The null-pitch conditioning idea is a simple, well-motivated fix for a real failure mode (text-camera entanglement) and is validated both qualitatively (Fig. 6) and quantitatively via a clean ablation (Table 2) showing consistent gains across metrics.

New evaluation benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme) fills a real gap, as existing benchmarks lack diverse pitch/roll coverage; benchmark construction methodology is reasonably described and the authors commit to releasing it.

Quantitative results show consistent, sizeable improvements over reasonable and relevant baselines (AC3D, AC3D+absolute Plücker, PreciseCam+WAN) on the camera-control metrics (pitch error, gravity error, relative rotation error), with plausible qualitative examples supporting the numbers.
Reasonable coverage of related work and proper positioning relative to Plücker-ray-based and point-cloud-based camera control methods.
weaknesses: Training data scale is very limited (only ~2K 360° videos from WEB360), which the authors themselves note likely explains worse FID/FVD/CLIP scores relative to AC3D trained on 65K videos; this makes it hard to disentangle whether gains come from the proposed representation/method versus differences in data distribution and scale, weakening the causal claims.

The core technical contribution is primarily a data-processing/annotation pipeline (gravity-alignment via 360° video + null-pitch captioning) layered onto an existing ControlNet architecture (from AC3D) and backbone (CogVideoX-2B); the architectural/algorithmic novelty is limited, which may be acceptable for a data-centric contribution but is not clearly framed as such in the contribution list.

No qualitative or quantitative evaluation of temporal smoothness or trajectory consistency beyond per-frame absolute pose metrics; potential jitter or discontinuities introduced by the random rotation sampling (Algorithm 1) are not analyzed.

The benchmark construction involves substantial manual filtering (140 videos hand-selected from 371K after visually verifying pitch estimation), raising concerns about reproducibility, potential selection bias, and the statistical power of only 140 evaluation videos.

Roll error is not directly evaluated (justified as unreliable near poles), and is only indirectly captured via gravity error, leaving a gap in the evaluation of one of the two key claimed capabilities (pitch and roll).

Only one backbone (CogVideoX-2B) is evaluated in the main paper; WAN backbone results are deferred to supplementary material, limiting the ability to assess generality of the approach within the main text.

Ablation study is limited to a single component (null-pitch conditioning); other design choices (e.g., the specific rotation-sampling algorithm parameters, 50% null-pitch ratio, choice of VLM captioner) are not ablated, leaving open questions about sensitivity and design necessity.

The absolute yaw-free formulation (gravity fixes pitch/roll but not yaw) is a reasonable practical choice but somewhat limits the generality of "absolute" camera control claimed in the title/abstract, since full 6-DoF absolute pose is not achieved.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: existing camera-control video generation methods condition on relative (first-frame) poses, which are ambiguous and cannot express absolute orientation concepts like horizon level or extreme tilt. Framing this via a gravity-aligned reference is a sensible and clearly explained idea.

The panoramic-video sampling pipeline (extracting SfM poses from 360° equirectangular video and re-projecting with randomly sampled rotation trajectories) is a practical way to escape the strong forward-facing bias of conventional camera-control datasets such as RealEstate10K, and the resulting distributional comparison (Fig. 5) supports this claim.

Null-pitch conditioning is an intuitive and well-motivated fix to the text/camera entanglement problem (e.g., captioning a canonical forward crop rather than the rotated crop), and the ablation (Tab. 2, Fig. 6) shows a measurable, consistent benefit across all reported metrics.

The paper proposes a new evaluation benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme) targeting a real gap: no existing benchmark offers paired prompts/camera poses/reference videos with wide pitch and roll coverage, and the dataset construction methodology (pitch binning, Perspective Fields filtering, synthetic roll warping) is clearly described.

Quantitative results show consistent improvement on orientation-focused metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr, RotErr) relative to adapted baselines (AC3D+text, AC3D+abs. Plücker, PreciseCam+WAN), and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 7 are illustrative of the claimed behavior.
weaknesses: Training data scale is very small (~2K 360° videos from WEB360) compared to baselines (e.g., AC3D trained on 65K RealEstate10K clips), and this is explicitly used post-hoc to explain worse CLIP/FID/FVD scores; this confounds the comparison and makes it hard to isolate whether gains stem from the proposed absolute representation/null-pitch conditioning or merely from different training data composition and distribution.

The method only controls camera rotation; translation trajectories are inherited directly from the source SfM estimate and not synthesizable or user-specifiable, which is a substantial limitation for a method billed as enabling general "camera control," and is only briefly acknowledged in the Discussion as future work rather than analyzed for its practical impact.

Yaw remains fundamentally unconstrained/arbitrary in the proposed absolute reference, so the "absolute camera control" claim is really only absolute in two of three rotational DOF (pitch, roll); this nuance is stated but its implications for usability/control (e.g., users cannot specify a true world-referenced heading) are not discussed.

The evaluation benchmark, after filtering, contains only 140 videos, which is a fairly small test set for FID/FVD-type metrics known to require larger sample sizes for stable estimates; no confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for Table 1 or Table 2.

Core geometric metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr, RotErr) rely on outputs of other learned models (Perspective Fields, VGGT) as pseudo-ground-truth on generated (not real) videos, introducing compounding estimation noise that is not quantified or validated against any ground truth/human judgment; no user study is conducted despite the paper's emphasis on cinematic/qualitative viewpoint fidelity.

Baselines are partially re-purposed/modified by the authors (e.g., "AC3D + cam. text.", "AC3D + cam. text. + abs. Plücker") rather than being the methods' originally intended use cases, which risks constructing comparisons that are not entirely fair reconstructions of the strongest possible competing approach.

Important methodological details are deferred entirely to supplementary material not included here (e.g., the exact definition of φ(·) used to establish the gravity-aligned frame, WAN backbone results, full benchmark construction and rotation sampling for test trajectories), making it difficult to fully verify central claims and reproducibility from the main text alone.

Visible qualitative artifacts (e.g., distorted crowds in Fig. 7) and the acknowledged drop in FID/FVD suggest the absolute conditioning strategy may trade off generation quality for control fidelity, but this trade-off is not thoroughly analyzed (e.g., no sweep over null-pitch ratio beyond the chosen 50%, no ablation on FoV/trajectory sampling design choices in Algorithm 1).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing camera-controlled video generation methods (e.g., AC3D, CameraCtrl) encode motion relative to the first frame, making absolute, physically grounded control (e.g., replicating a specific pitch/roll with respect to gravity) impossible. The gravity-referenced formulation is a clear, well-motivated conceptual contribution.

The data pipeline that mines 360° panoramic videos to synthesize diverse, gravity-annotated camera trajectories (including rare shots such as Dutch angles or extreme pitch) is a creative way to escape the strong forward-facing bias of conventional video capture datasets, and is clearly illustrated (Fig. 4, Fig. 5 distribution comparisons).

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, well-justified annotation strategy for disentangling text semantics from camera orientation, and the ablation (Table 2, Fig. 6) convincingly shows it improves both quantitative accuracy and qualitative correctness.

The paper contributes a new, needed evaluation benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme) with near-uniform pitch/roll coverage, filling an evaluation gap since prior benchmarks (RealEstate10K splits) lack angular diversity; the authors commit to releasing it.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation protocol combining absolute orientation metrics (pitch/gravity error), relative rotation/translation error, and standard generation-quality metrics (CLIP, FID, FVD), tested against multiple sensible baselines (AC3D variants, PreciseCam+WAN).

Quantitative results show sizeable, consistent improvements in the camera-control-specific metrics (nearly halving pitch/gravity error and substantially reducing relative rotation error) over baselines, supported by qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The proposed control is restricted to rotation only; translation trajectories are inherited unchanged from the source video/panorama rather than being independently controllable, which somewhat limits the claim of full "camera trajectory" control and should be foregrounded as a core limitation rather than deferred to a brief discussion paragraph.

Yaw remains unconstrained/arbitrary in the gravity-aligned frame, so the method is not truly a full 6-DoF absolute control system—this should be stated explicitly and earlier, since the abstract/intro language ("precise and interpretable control over camera parameters") could be read as more general than what is actually delivered.

The comparison against AC3D is confounded by differing training data scale (65k RealEstate10K videos vs. only ~2K WEB360 panoramas); the authors acknowledge this to explain worse FID/FVD, but it also complicates attributing the gains in pose accuracy purely to the gravity-referenced representation versus simply having more diverse rotational training data. A more controlled ablation (e.g., training AC3D's relative representation on the exact same panorama-derived dataset) would better isolate the contribution of the absolute/gravity formulation itself.

Evaluation metrics for orientation (pitch, gravity error) rely on Perspective Fields, the same class of geometric estimator plausibly related to tools used elsewhere in the pipeline; potential circularity or estimator bias in both benchmark construction and evaluation is not discussed.

The benchmark, after manual filtering, comprises only 140 videos, and roll variation is synthetically injected via video warping rather than being naturally captured, which may introduce warping artifacts that affect FID/FVD and are not clearly disentangled from generation quality effects.

Experiments are conducted primarily on a single, relatively small/older backbone (CogVideoX-2B); WAN backbone results are relegated to supplementary material, leaving the main paper's evidence for generalization across architectures thin.

No user study or human perceptual evaluation is included to corroborate that the qualitative cinematic improvements (e.g., correct low-angle/high-roll shots) are perceived as such by viewers, despite the paper's framing around enabling cinematic storyboarding.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: absolute, gravity-grounded camera control for extreme rotations (pitch/roll) in text-to-video generation, going beyond the modest, relative-to-first-frame trajectories supported by prior work like AC3D and CameraCtrl.

The data pipeline is a clever and technically sound way to sidestep the lack of gravity-annotated large-scale video data: it derives absolute poses by combining SfM-estimated relative poses on 360° panoramic videos with single-image gravity/up-vector estimation, and then re-samples camera crops (Algorithm 1) to obtain a much more diverse distribution of viewpoints (including barrel rolls, extreme pitch) than naturally captured video datasets.

The null-pitch conditioning idea for disentangling caption semantics from camera orientation is a simple but effective and non-obvious contribution, directly targeting a real failure mode (models overriding camera specification when content clashes with viewing direction), and is separately validated in an ablation and in a dedicated entanglement benchmark (PolyHaven-based).

Two new benchmarks are introduced (SpatialVID-extreme for absolute orientation coverage, and a PolyHaven-based prompt-camera entanglement benchmark), which fill a real gap since existing test splits such as RealEstate10K have very limited pitch/roll diversity; the authors commit to releasing these test sets.

Quantitative results show consistent, sizable improvements on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) and relative rotation error versus multiple relevant baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam combinations), and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 2 and Fig. 5 visibly support the claim that competing methods fail at extreme rotations while the proposed method tracks the intended trajectory.

The ablation isolating null-pitch conditioning (Table 1, and Fig. 6) demonstrates a large, consistent improvement (67%/52% reduction in pitch/gravity error) supporting the causal claim linking this design choice to the observed benefit.
weaknesses: CLIP score is worse than nearly every baseline (Table 1) and the paper's explanation (entanglement/correct suppression of conflicting content) is plausible but not rigorously disentangled from possible degraded semantic fidelity or caption drift caused by training on null-pitch captions rather than the true crop content; a more careful human or VLM-based semantic-fidelity study beyond the small 20-scene PolyHaven set would strengthen this claim.

FID scores for the proposed method are worse than most baselines and FVD is only "competitive"/middling, suggesting a possible trade-off between camera controllability and generation quality/realism that is not deeply analyzed or discussed (e.g., no ablation isolating whether this stems from the null-pitch strategy, the synthetic panorama-derived training data domain gap, or backbone finetuning).

Translation control is inherited directly from source video trajectories and the on-the-fly augmentation pipeline is restricted to rotation only; translation diversity/extremes (e.g., large forward moves, arbitrary 3D paths) are not covered by the core data-augmentation contribution, limiting the scope of "absolute camera control" to primarily rotational aspects, which is acknowledged as a limitation but somewhat undercuts the generality of the title/framing.

Substantial reliance on a chain of pretrained estimators (SfM pose estimation via ViPE, gravity/up-vector estimation via Perspective Fields, VLM captioning) introduces compounding potential noise sources into the training data and evaluation metrics themselves (e.g., PitchErr/GravityErr are computed using the same Perspective Fields model used to construct training/benchmark data), raising a possible circularity concern that is not explicitly addressed.

Benchmark curation involves significant manual filtering (e.g., manually filtering to 140 videos with uniform pitch from SpatialVID-HQ, discarding 38% of PanoVid training data) which, while reasonable, introduces subjective selection biases that are not quantified, and the resulting benchmarks are relatively small in scale (140 videos; 380 prompt-pitch pairs across 20 scenes for entanglement) for drawing broad conclusions.

Some baselines are arguably not optimally tuned analogues (e.g., AC3D and PreciseCam were not designed for this exact task and are adapted via prompt engineering or pipeline composition), which is reasonable given the lack of established competitors but leaves open whether comparisons fully reflect each baseline's best-case capability.

The paper is dense with many pipeline components (SfM, gravity estimation, null-pitch/look-down captioning, CFG negative prompting) whose interactions and individual necessity are only partially ablated (only null-pitch conditioning is ablated in the main paper), making it harder to assess which design choices are essential versus incidental to the overall gains.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored limitation of camera-controlled video generation: extreme rotations (large pitch/roll, 180° flips) that existing relative Plücker-based methods cannot handle.

The core idea of using calibrated 360° panoramic videos plus estimated gravity direction to synthesize training data with full-sphere camera coverage is a sensible and creative way to work around the strong forward-facing bias of conventional video datasets.

Null-pitch conditioning is a well-motivated and simple fix for text-camera entanglement, and the paper includes a targeted ablation (Table 1) and a dedicated entanglement benchmark (Fig. 6) that convincingly demonstrate its effect on pitch error and CLIP alignment.

The paper proposes two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) that could be useful community resources given the lack of standard evaluation protocols for extreme camera control.

Reasonably broad baseline comparison, including a concurrent gravity-aware method (UCPE) and several adapted baselines (AC3D+text, PreciseCam+GEN3C/WAN), plus qualitative figures that visually support the orientation-accuracy claims.
weaknesses: Quantitative results are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: the method is worse than several baselines on FID, FVD, and CLIP (Table 1), and only clearly wins on the orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr, RotErr) that the method is explicitly designed to optimize, which risks a somewhat self-serving comparison.

The training/evaluation pipeline is built on cascades of imperfect estimators (SfM/ViPE poses, Perspective Fields for gravity/pitch, VGGT for rotation error), and the same or similar estimators are used both to construct training data/benchmarks and to compute evaluation metrics, raising concerns about circularity and about how much reported gains reflect genuine visual quality versus alignment with the estimators' biases.

The training set is small and narrow after filtering (4,798 YouTube panoramic videos, 38% discarded), which limits scene diversity relative to standard large-scale video training corpora and raises questions about generalization to typical text-to-video content and dynamic scenes beyond what panorama-derived crops can represent.

Camera control is restricted to rotation; translation is inherited passively from the source panoramic videos rather than being independently controllable/learned, which somewhat undercuts the "full absolute camera control" framing showcased in the teaser (e.g., combined pitch sweep with 8m forward translation) and is only acknowledged as future work.

The SpatialVID-extreme benchmark relies on manual filtering down to 140 videos with uniform pitch and on synthetically added roll via video warping (introducing warping artifacts), which may bias FID/FVD comparisons and limits the benchmark's realism and scale.

No human/user study is included to validate perceptual quality or camera-control fidelity, despite the paper's emphasis on cinematic usability for content creators; the analysis relies entirely on automatic proxy metrics whose reliability near poles is itself noted as unreliable for roll.

Baseline adaptations (e.g., AC3D+camera text appended via template, PreciseCam initial frame + WAN-I2V) are somewhat ad hoc reconfigurations of methods not designed for this exact setting, making it unclear whether the comparison isolates the proposed contributions or simply reflects the baselines' inherent mismatch to the task.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored limitation in text-to-video camera control: existing methods use relative/ambiguous representations and fail on extreme rotations (e.g., large pitch, roll, 180° turns); this paper proposes a well-motivated gravity-aligned absolute coordinate framework to resolve this.

The data pipeline that samples diverse synthetic camera trajectories from 360° panoramic video (with SfM pose estimation and gravity-alignment) is a creative and effective way to overcome the strong bias toward forward-facing, near-horizontal viewpoints in conventional video datasets, and is clearly described with sufficient technical detail (Sec. 3.2, Algorithm 1, Fig. 3-4).

The null-pitch conditioning strategy for disentangling prompt semantics from camera orientation is a simple but effective idea, and the ablation (Table 1) convincingly demonstrates its impact, with 67%/52% reductions in pitch/gravity error when included.

Two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme for extreme-angle video generation, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) fill a clear gap, since no prior benchmark provides paired text/camera/video data with diverse pitch and roll coverage; the construction methodology (pitch-binning, filtering, synthetic roll augmentation) is reasonably described.

Quantitative results show consistent and fairly large improvements over multiple relevant baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam-based pipelines) on absolute and relative orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr, RotErr), and qualitative examples (Fig. 2, 5, 6) visibly support the claimed improvements in extreme-viewpoint fidelity and reduced prompt-camera entanglement.

The related work section is thorough and clearly situates the contribution relative to concurrent work (e.g., UCPE), image-based camera control (PreciseCam), and camera pose/gravity estimation literature.
weaknesses: The proposed method underperforms several baselines on CLIP score and does not improve FID over baselines; while the CLIP drop is explained by desired prompt-camera disentanglement, this argument is only partially validated (via the entanglement benchmark) and the FID/FVD trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

Ablations are limited to a single component (null-pitch conditioning); other design choices such as the look-down negative-prompting strategy, data filtering thresholds (38% of videos discarded), FoV sampling scheme, and pole-biased viewpoint sampling are not individually ablated, making it hard to assess their individual contributions.

Comparisons to baselines may not be entirely apples-to-apples: AC3D uses a smaller CogVideoX-2B backbone while the proposed method fine-tunes a larger WAN-2.2 5B model, and PreciseCam+GEN3C is explicitly noted as unable to generate dynamic content; capacity/backbone differences could partially explain performance gaps and are not controlled for.

Camera control is currently restricted to rotation augmentation only; translation is inherited from the original source video and cannot be freely synthesized, which is an important practical limitation for full 6-DoF camera control (acknowledged by the authors as future work).

No human/user study is included to assess perceptual video quality or the practical usability of extreme camera control for creative workflows, which would strengthen claims of qualitative superiority beyond automated metrics and the shown qualitative examples.

Reliance on estimated gravity/pose annotations (from SfM and single-image gravity estimators) introduces potential label noise; while filtering removes clearly failed cases, the residual noise in retained pseudo-labels and its effect on model training is not quantitatively analyzed.

The two new benchmarks are constructed and curated by the same authors proposing the method, which, while transparently described, introduces some risk of benchmark design choices favoring the proposed approach; independent validation or community adoption would strengthen confidence in benchmark neutrality.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored limitation in existing camera-controlled video generation: reliance on first-frame-relative camera representations that cannot express absolute orientation w.r.t. gravity, preventing extreme pitch/roll control.

The 360° panoramic video data pipeline is a clever and practical solution to the lack of training data with extreme camera angles, enabling sampling across the full sphere of viewpoints rather than the narrow forward-facing distribution of conventional video datasets.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, well-motivated fix for the prompt-camera entanglement problem, and the ablations (Table 1, Fig. 6) convincingly show it substantially improves absolute orientation accuracy and reduces reliance on prompt semantics at extreme angles.

Method is shown to generalize across multiple conditioning schemes (UCPE, Plücker) and multiple backbone architectures (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B), strengthening the claim that the contribution is a general strategy rather than an architecture-specific trick.

Two new, carefully constructed benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme for camera control under extreme angles, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) fill a real gap, since standard datasets like RealEstate10K lack diversity in pitch/roll, and these are planned for release.

Quantitative results show clear and consistent improvements in absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) over all tested baselines, and competitive/near-best relative rotation accuracy, backed by informative qualitative examples showing failure modes of prior work.

Reasonable coverage of related work and clear articulation of how the proposed absolute, gravity-anchored representation differs from concurrent work (UCPE) and prior relative-conditioning methods (AC3D, PRoPE).
weaknesses: Improved camera control accuracy consistently comes at the cost of lower CLIP score and often worse/similar FID and FVD compared to baselines; this trade-off between control fidelity and generation quality/text alignment is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed or mitigated.

The training data pipeline depends on multiple estimated quantities (SfM pose via ViPE, gravity/up-vector via Perspective Fields), and a large fraction of source videos (38%) had to be discarded due to unreliable pose estimates, raising concerns about noise propagation and the practical robustness/scalability of the annotation pipeline.

The evaluation datasets are fairly small (138 videos for the extreme-angle benchmark, 20 panoramas / 380 prompt-pitch pairs for the entanglement benchmark), which limits the statistical confidence of the reported metrics, especially given the inherent noisiness of learned pose/orientation estimators used as pseudo ground truth (VGGT, Perspective Fields).

Camera translation is still limited to reusing translations from the original panoramic source videos rather than being freely sampled, so the method’s claimed "absolute camera control" is asymmetric — rotation is fully controllable while translation diversity/augmentation remains an open limitation.

The training panoramic corpus (YouTube subset of PanoVid) likely has its own domain biases (e.g., travel/scenic content), and the paper does not thoroughly analyze how this domain gap affects generalization to more varied video content (e.g., indoor scenes, human-centric activities) beyond a few qualitative examples.

No human/user study is included to validate perceptual quality or the practical usefulness of the extreme camera control capability, relying solely on automated metrics that themselves depend on imperfect off-the-shelf estimators.

Some baseline comparisons involve adaptations outside the baselines' original training distribution (e.g., feeding AC3D absolute Plücker rays, or text-based absolute camera descriptions), which, while disclosed, could make comparisons less fair or harder to interpret.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: existing camera-conditioned video diffusion methods typically encode trajectories relative to the first frame, making it impossible to specify absolute orientation (e.g., pointing at the sky) or to generalize to extreme pitches/rolls that are out-of-distribution for human-captured footage.

The gravity-aligned data generation pipeline (extracting SfM poses from 360° panoramic video, estimating gravity via up-vector averaging across yaw-sampled crops, then sampling diverse synthetic rotation trajectories via Algorithm 1) is a reasonable and fairly detailed engineering solution to the lack of gravity-annotated training data, and is demonstrated to work across multiple camera-conditioning schemes (UCPE, Plücker) and backbones (CogVideoX, WAN-2.1, WAN-2.2).

Null-pitch conditioning is a sensible and clearly motivated idea to reduce prompt/camera-angle entanglement, and the ablations (Table 1, Fig. 6) convincingly show it substantially reduces pitch/gravity error and improves alignment at extreme angles.

The paper contributes two new evaluation protocols (SpatialVID-extreme for extreme-angle generation, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) that could be useful community resources given the current lack of standardized evaluation for this capability.

Reasonably broad set of baselines (AC3D, PreciseCam+WAN, PreciseCam+GEN3C, UCPE) and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 2, Fig. 5) show clear qualitative advantages in handling extreme rotations compared to prior work.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is primarily a data-curation/training pipeline and captioning heuristic rather than a new modeling or architectural advance; the actual conditioning mechanisms (UCPE, Plücker rays) are adopted directly from prior work, which somewhat limits the method's novelty as an 'algorithm' contribution.

Image/video quality metrics (FID, FVD) are not improved and in several configurations are worse than baselines (e.g., WAN-2.2 5B variant has the best orientation metrics but among the worst FVD), and CLIP score is consistently lower for the proposed method; the paper attributes this to deliberate prompt/camera disentanglement, but this is a self-serving post-hoc explanation without an independent human study confirming perceptual quality or correctness is actually preserved.

Quantitative evaluation relies heavily on other learned models as pseudo-ground-truth (Perspective Fields for pitch/gravity error, VGGT for rotation error), raising concerns about circularity/bias, since errors in these estimators (particularly near poles, acknowledged by the authors for roll) could systematically favor or penalize certain generation styles rather than reflecting true geometric fidelity.

The two proposed benchmarks are small and manually curated (138 videos for SpatialVID-extreme after heavy manual filtering of pitch estimates; only 20 panoramas/380 prompt-pitch pairs for the entanglement benchmark), limiting statistical reliability of the reported differences and raising reproducibility concerns until the promised release.

Despite the abstract and Fig. 1 emphasizing translation control, the method's data augmentation is restricted to rotations only; translations are inherited unmodified from the source panoramic videos (acknowledged as a limitation), so the degree of genuine 'absolute' translation control demonstrated is more limited than implied by the framing.

Several engineering choices (the look-down negative-prompt trick to suppress tripod/selfie-stick artifacts, manual filtering of failed pose estimates, discarding 38% of training videos) suggest the pipeline is somewhat ad hoc and dataset-specific, raising questions about generalization to other panorama sources or video backbones without substantial re-tuning.

No comparison (quantitative) against panorama-generation-based approaches (360DVD, PanoWan) that could achieve gravity-aligned control via cropping, despite these being discussed at length in related work; only qualitative claims are made about their downsides in the supplementary.

Fair baseline adaptation is questionable in places, e.g., AC3D is given absolute pitch/roll only through a text template, which is arguably not a fair or well-tuned use of that architecture, potentially inflating the apparent gap between the proposed method and baselines.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: precise, absolute (gravity-referenced) camera control in text-to-video generation, especially for extreme pitch/roll trajectories that existing relative-encoding methods cannot handle.

Novel data pipeline that extracts gravity-aligned absolute camera poses from 360° panoramic video via SfM + up-vector estimation, and samples diverse camera rotation trajectories on the sphere (Algorithm 1), providing a principled way to overcome the strong forward-facing bias of existing video training data.

The null-pitch conditioning idea (captioning with a forward-facing crop rather than the extreme-angle crop) is a simple but effective and non-obvious insight for disentangling prompt semantics from camera pose, and the paper provides a dedicated benchmark and ablation (Fig. 6, Sec 4.6) that convincingly demonstrates its benefit.

Method is demonstrated to be modular/backbone-agnostic, being applied across multiple architectures (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B) and two camera encodings (UCPE, Plücker), with consistent improvements over strong recent baselines (AC3D, UCPE, PreciseCam+WAN, PreciseCam+GEN3C).

Introduces two new benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme for absolute orientation evaluation, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) that address the lack of existing evaluation protocols for extreme camera angles, which could be valuable for future community use if released as promised.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of null-pitch conditioning and absolute (vs relative) camera conditioning, showing substantial, consistent gains across metrics and backbones.

Qualitative results (Figs. 2, 5, 6) are compelling and clearly illustrate failure modes of baselines (e.g., generating wrong content under conflicting prompt/camera cues) versus the proposed method's fidelity to specified camera orientation.
weaknesses: FID/FVD scores for the proposed method are often worse than or comparable to weaker baselines (e.g., PreciseCam+WAN has notably better FVD in the WAN-2.1 1.3B setting, 776.3 vs 1041.6), and CLIP scores are consistently lower for the proposed method; the paper attributes this partly to correct behavior under entanglement, but a more rigorous quantitative decomposition (beyond the qualitative Fig. 6 CLIP-to-groundtruth-caption metric) would strengthen this claim across the main benchmark, not just the small 20-scene entanglement set.

The training/evaluation data pipeline relies on several imperfect off-the-shelf components (ViPE pose estimation, Perspective Fields gravity estimation, InternVL captioning, VGGT for RotErr evaluation) whose errors could propagate into both training data quality and evaluation metrics; no analysis of these components' error rates or sensitivity is provided.

Substantial data filtering was needed (38% of videos discarded) and the final training corpus (4798 panoramic videos) is relatively small in absolute terms; scaling behavior and dataset size effects are not studied.

Translation is inherited directly from the source panoramic videos and cannot be freely resampled/augmented (acknowledged as a limitation), limiting the diversity of camera translation trajectories compared to the exhaustive rotation sampling.

The SpatialVID-extreme benchmark's roll dimension is synthetically added via video warping rather than sourced from real 3D camera motion, which may not fully reflect realistic roll dynamics or associated visual artifacts (e.g., warping artifacts near frame borders) that could confound FID/FVD comparisons.

Some comparisons may be somewhat unfair to baselines not designed for absolute/extreme control (e.g., AC3D is fed absolute pose info via text as a workaround), which, while transparently disclosed, makes some of the quantitative margins less directly interpretable as method superiority versus a distribution-shift effect.
No explicit computational cost/efficiency comparison (training time, inference latency, parameter counts) across the different backbone variants, which would help gauge practical applicability.
